displayedInputs.question:
Problems \(8,\) \(9,\) and \(10\) use the data found in the accompanying paragraph and figures.

Bake Sale

Four friends, Art, Roger, Paul and Trisha, bake cookies, and all cookies have the same thickness. The shapes of the cookies differ, as shown.

• Art’s cookies are trapezoids:

[Figure 1](attached-image-1)

• Roger’s cookies are rectangles:

[Figure 2](attached-image-2)

• Paul’s cookies are parallelograms:

[Figure 3](attached-image-3)

• Trisha’s cookies are triangles:

[Figure 4](attached-image-4)

Each friend uses the same amount of dough, and Art makes exactly \(12\) cookies.

Art’s cookies sell for \(60\)¢ each. To earn the same amount from a single batch, how much should one of Roger’s cookies cost?

mappings.rationale: Calculate the trapezoid and rectangle areas. Equal dough amounts and equal thickness imply equal total cookie area per batch, allowing proportional reasoning about cookie counts and prices for equal revenue. The parallelogram and triangle figures are not needed.
mappings.answerReason: Art's cookie area is (3+5)×3/2=12 square inches; Roger's is 4×2=8 square inches. The batch therefore has total area 12×12=144 square inches, giving Roger 144/8=18 cookies. To match Art's revenue of 12×60=720 cents, each must cost 720/18=40 cents.
